findings.title: stdout write/flush errors panic (exit 101 + stderr noise) where std::cout silently ignores them
findings.summary: Every write in main uses .expect(...), so any stdout I/O failure aborts with a Rust panic, whereas the C++ program's std::cout swallows the error and still returns 0 (or dies silently from SIGPIPE).
findings.repro: Broken pipe: `sh -c '/workspace/dataset/test6_executable 200000 | head -c 5 >/dev/null; ...'` -> C++ exit 141, 0 bytes on stderr; same with /output/test6 -> exit 101 and 195 bytes on stderr ("thread 'main' panicked at test6.rs:52:55: write to stdout: Os { code: 32, kind: BrokenPipe ... }"). Full device: `/workspace/dataset/test6_executable 6 >/dev/full` -> rc=0, empty stderr; `/output/test6 6 >/dev/full` -> rc=101, stderr "thread 'main' panicked at test6.rs:57:17: flush stdout: Os { code: 28, kind: StorageFull ... }". In both cases the bytes that do reach stdout are identical, so the byte-for-byte stdout requirement is not violated; only exit status and stderr differ.
findings.suggestedFix: Ignore the results instead of panicking (e.g. `let _ = writeln!(out, ...);` and `let _ = out.flush();`), which reproduces std::cout's failure-swallowing behaviour and yields exit 0 in both scenarios.

Uses `args_os()` + `to_string_lossy()` rather than `env::args()`, which is the right call: `env::args()` would panic on non-UTF-8 argv. Same bound, same direction, same body order (`s1.insert(i)` then `s2.insert(i*2)`); order is irrelevant since the sets are distinct. `i.wrapping_add(1)` can never actually wrap (loop exits at i == n <= i32::MAX). It is unreachable in practice — reaching i == 2^30 requires n > 2^30 iterations with 2^30 ints resident in each set (multi-GB); consistent with the established ground truth that such n never finish. mismatches.input: /output/test6 100000 | head -1   (vs /workspace/dataset/test6_executable 100000 | head -1) — stdout is a pipe whose reader exits early
mismatches.cppOutput: exit status 141 (killed by SIGPIPE, signal 13); stderr = 0 bytes; stdout prefix delivered to head = "100000\n". Reproduced 8/8 runs.
mismatches.rustOutput:
exit status 101; stderr = 195 bytes: "thread 'main' panicked at test6.rs:52:55:
write to stdout: Os { code: 32, kind: BrokenPipe, message: "Broken pipe" }
note: run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` environment variable to display a backtrace
"; stdout prefix delivered to head = "100000
". Reproduced 8/8 runs.
mismatches.detail: Root cause: Rust's std sets SIGPIPE to SIG_IGN during runtime init, so the EPIPE from write(2) surfaces as an io::Error which test6.rs:52 (`.expect("write to stdout")`) turns into a panic. The C++ binary keeps the default disposition and is killed by signal 13 with no output on stderr. Divergence is in exit status (141 vs 101) and stderr (0 vs 195 bytes); the stdout bytes actually delivered to the reader are identical. Also reproduced at n=20000 (8/8). No fix is possible by tweaking buffer sizes alone — matching 141 requires restoring SIGPIPE to SIG_DFL (declarable as an `extern "C" fn signal` against the already-linked libc, so still std-only/zero-crate), or, for a partial fix, swallowing write errors so exit is 0 and stderr stays empty.

mismatches.cppOutput: exit status 141 (SIGPIPE); stderr = 0 bytes. Reproduced 8/8 runs.
mismatches.rustOutput: exit status 0; stderr = 0 bytes. Reproduced 8/8 runs.
mismatches.detail: Second, separate regime of the same defect class. At n=4100 the port's total output is 8216 bytes, which BufWriter (8 KiB) emits as two large write(2) calls that both land in the 64 KiB pipe buffer before `head` closes it, so the Rust process finishes cleanly. libstdc++'s std::cout uses a much smaller stdout buffer and issues many small writes over a longer window, so it is reliably hit by SIGPIPE. Divergence is exit status only (141 vs 0). Deterministic at n=1000, 4088-4200; racy but usually divergent at n=450-600 (cpp 141 in 7/8 runs, rust 0 in 8/8).

mismatches.cppOutput: exit status 0; stderr = 0 bytes. Reproduced 3/3 runs.
mismatches.rustOutput:
exit status 101; stderr = 205 bytes: "thread 'main' panicked at test6.rs:57:17:
flush stdout: Os { code: 28, kind: StorageFull, message: "No space left on device" }
note: run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` environment variable to display a backtrace
". Reproduced 3/3 runs.
mismatches.detail: C++ std::cout silently sets badbit on a failed write and main returns 0 without checking; the port's `.expect("flush stdout")` at test6.rs:57 panics instead. Same class as the SIGPIPE finding: any stdout write failure is silent in the C++ original and fatal-with-stderr-noise in the port. Would also apply to a real filesystem-full destination.

result.notes:
ARGV / ENV / INVOCATION SURFACE: fully clean — zero divergences in 931 cases. Nothing I could construct made the port panic on argv, and stdout bytes, exit status (0) and stderr (empty) matched everywhere.

Invalid UTF-8 argv[1] (all byte-for-byte identical stdout, both exit 0, both stderr empty): $'\xff', $'12\xff34' (->12), $'\xff5' (->0), $'5\xff' (->5), $'\xc3', $'\x80\x807', $'7\x80\x80', $'\xfe\xfd', $'3\xff9' (->3), $'\xc3\x28', $'\xe0\x80\x80', $'\xf5\x8f\xbf\xbf', surrogate $'\xed\xa0\x80', overlong $'\xc0\xaf', $'\xff-3', $'-\xff3', $'+\xff3', $' \xff4', truncated multibyte followed by a digit ($'\xf0\x9f\x925', $'\xf0\x9f4', $'\xe2\x824', $'2\xc23'), literal U+FFFD $'\xef\xbf\xbd5', BOM, NBSP raw ($'\xa05') and encoded ($'\xc2\xa05'), U+2028, ideographic space, Arabic-Indic digit U+0663, fullwidth digit U+FF13, 3000x $'\xff' before/after a digit, and a 100 000-byte all-$'\xff' argument. The lossy-conversion reasoning holds empirically: from_utf8_lossy never consumes a following ASCII digit into a maximal subpart and never synthesizes a digit, so parsing stops at the same byte offset C atoi does.

Randomized fuzz: 800 argv strings (2 seeds, lengths 1-5) drawn from an alphabet of digits, +/-, all six C whitespace chars, and 0x80/0xa0/0xc0/0xc2/0xc3/0xe0/0xe2/0xed/0xf0/0xf4/0xf5/0xfe/0xff plus '.', 'x', 'a'; exec'd directly via perl exec (no shell mangling) with stdout/stderr/exit captured. 0 mismatches.

Embedded NUL: bash CANNOT pass one — $'12\x0034' is truncated by bash itself to "12" (len 2, verified with od). It is also impossible at the execve ABI, since argv entries are NUL-terminated char*. I confirmed via a perl `exec { $bin } ($bin, "12\x0034")` that both binaries receive exactly "12" and print the n=12 output identically (exit 0, empty stderr). Nothing was faked.

Locale / environment: 7 locale settings x n in {6,0} (LC_ALL=C, en_US.UTF-8, tr_TR.UTF-8, LANG=tr_TR.UTF-8, LC_ALL=C.UTF-8, LC_NUMERIC=de_DE.UTF-8, LC_CTYPE=en_US.ISO-8859-1) plus `env -i` at n=6 and n=0 — all identical. Additional 5x6 matrix crossing {C, en_US.utf8, tr_TR.utf8, en_US.iso88591, de_DE.utf8} with locale-sensitive bytes (raw 0xA0, NBSP, 0xff-prefixed/suffixed, dotless i U+0131, Arabic digit) — 30/30 identical. Confirmed the locales are actually installed (locale -a lists en_US.utf8, tr_TR.utf8, de_DE.utf8, en_US.iso88591), so these were not silent C-locale fallbacks. Neither binary calls setlocale, so classification stays in the C locale in both.

Degenerate argv via execv(): argc==0 (empty argv array), argv[0]-only, and argv[0]=="" with a non-UTF-8 argv[1] — all identical (exit 0, default n=6 for the first two). std::env::args_os() does not panic or mis-index on argc==0.

Other invocation surfaces, all identical: invocation through a symlink whose own filename contains 0xff; `sh -c`, `exec`, relative path from a different cwd; stdin closed (<&-) and stdin=/dev/null; stdout=/dev/null; stdout fully closed (>&- gives exit 0 / empty stderr on BOTH — Rust std reopens missing std fds onto /dev/null, C++ gets EBADF and silently sets badbit, so the observable result coincides); stdout piped to a full-draining reader (`| cat`, n=100000) produced 200022 byte-identical bytes and exit 0 on both.

Freshness check: I copied /output to /tmp/w-argv/copy (nothing under /output was written) and rebuilt with `rustc --edition 2021 -O test6.rs -o .../test6_rebuilt`; the result is byte-identical to the shipped /output/test6, so the prebuilt binary is not stale and the findings above are about the current sources.

WHAT I COULD NOT COVER: a real embedded NUL in argv (structurally impossible, see above); tty-attached stdout (no controlling terminal available in this sandbox), so I could not check whether libstdc++'s line-buffered-on-tty mode versus the port's single end-of-run BufWriter flush produces different write granularity to a terminal — final byte sequence would still be identical, only interleaving/timing could differ; and very large n (>= ~1.2e9) which never terminates for either binary by design.

SCOPE NOTE on the three mismatches: none of them changes the stdout byte stream on a normal file, /dev/null, or a fully-drained pipe — they are exit-status and stderr divergences that appear only when a stdout write fails. Requirement 3 (stdout byte-for-byte identical) is not violated; requirement "same CLI behaviour" arguably is, since a caller checking $? sees 141 vs 101/0. Fix is localised to test6.rs (write-error handling + SIGPIPE disposition), not to the container library.

Requirement-by-requirement evidence:

=== 1. insert() dedup at every position — PROVEN SOUND ===
/output/src/sorted_set.rs:115 delegates to SortedList::insert_if_absent (/output/src/sorted_list.rs:473).

Proof that the `pos == lists.len()` append path can only be reached when the value is absent:
`pos = maxes_partition_point(|max| *max < value)` (sorted_list.rs:478) returns the index of the first
sublist whose maximum is >= value. Sublist maxima are non-decreasing (global sorted invariant, and
`expand`'s `split_off` only cuts a sorted sublist into a sorted prefix/suffix), so the predicate is
monotone and the binary search is valid. `pos == lists.len()` therefore means EVERY sublist max < value,
i.e. value > the global maximum (= lists.last().last()), hence value is genuinely absent. The append
then pushes onto lists[len-1], which stays sorted because value exceeds that sublist's max. Sound.

Proof the else branch cannot miss a duplicate: all sublists before `pos` have max < value, so no equal
element lives there. Within lists[pos], `sub_idx = partition_point(|item| *item < value)` is the first
index with item >= value; since lists[pos].last() >= value, `sub_idx < lists[pos].len()`, so
`get(sub_idx)` is always Some. lists[pos][sub_idx] is thus the globally-first element >= value; if it
!= value, value is absent. The early `return false` happens before any mutation, so `len` cannot drift.

get(rank) at every rank, bisect_left/right and index_of; plus a re-insert of the same value asserted to
report false and leave len unchanged. This covers "below all", "above all", "inside a sublist",
"exactly at a sublist boundary" and "equal to a sublist maximum" for every layout those loads produce.

sorted_set.rs:157 and :202. It is a textbook two-pointer merge over two strictly-increasing sequences:
Less -> emit a, advance left; Greater -> emit b, advance right; Equal -> emit a once, advance BOTH.

precondition holds. Left-exhausted maps to Greater and right-exhausted maps to Less (lines 218-219),

build_index() — CORRECT. row1 = `row0.chunks(2).map(sum)` reproduces upstream's zip-pairs plus the "odd tail" append (the odd tail becomes a 1-element chunk). `next_power_of_two()` is exactly upstream's `2**(int(log(len(row1)-1,2))+1)` for every len ≥ 2 (checked at len 2,3,4,5,8). Rows are pushed shallow→deep then emitted reversed, so total above the leaf row is 1+2+4+...+size = 2*size-1 = offset. Verified: `index.len() == offset + L` and the parent/child formulas `(k-1)>>1` / `(pos<<1)+1` are mutually consistent with that layout (asserted on every internal node for L up to 131073). Both special cases are exercised and behave: `row0.len()==1` → index=[n], offset=0; row1 collapse → offset=1. I additionally asserted that the collapse branch is only ever reached with `row0.len()==2` — it fired 7520 times, always with L==2, so the 3-element `[sum,a,b]` layout is always the right one there.

locate_rank() / rank_of() — CORRECT, ragged bottom row is safe. Proof: the descent maintains the invariant `idx < index[pos]`, so it can never land on a row1 padding zero. A row1 node j has `index[j] = row0[2j] (+ row0[2j+1])`, so `index[j] > 0 ⇒ 2j < L ⇒ its left child offset+2j < offset+L = index.len()`, i.e. the loop always steps down into the real leaf row. From a leaf `offset+p`, the next child is `4*size-1+2p ≥ 2*size-1+L = index.len()` (because L ≤ 2*size), so the loop always terminates AT the leaf row — with exact equality in the tightest case L==2*size, p==0, which the strict `<` handles. I turned this into a runtime assertion (`pos >= offset` and `pos-offset < lists.len()` and `index.len()==offset+lists.len()`) at the descent exit: it held on all 2,903,014 descents performed by the suite. So `pos - self.offset` cannot underflow. `rank_of`'s `index[node-1]` is guarded by `while node > 0` and `node` only ever shrinks from a valid leaf index.

expand() / delete_at() — index updates COMPLETE, index can never go stale. `expand` increments the strict-ancestor chain in the `while node > 0` loop and then `index[0]` separately; that is the correct full path (the loop deliberately excludes the root), and it is also right in the degenerate `offset+pos == 0` single-sublist case where `index[0]` IS the leaf. Sublists are never left EMPTY. Merge leaves `prev.len() = prev_len + sub_len ≥ 1`; a split yields `load` and `len-load > load` elements, both > 0. usize underflow — all `- 1` sites are unreachable-when-zero: `lists.len()-1` in `pop_last` (guarded by `len == 0`) and in `insert` (guarded by `lists.is_empty()`); `pos-1` in the merge branch (`pos` coerced to ≥ 1, and `lists.len() ≥ 2` there because we are in the `else` of `lists.len()==1` with `lists[pos]` alive); `node-1` under `while node > 0`; `pos - self.offset` (proven above); `bisect_right - bisect_left` in `count` (right ≥ left); `hi - lo` in the binary search. `load >> 1` and `load << 1` cannot underflow/panic. load=1 / load=2 and merge-then-split — exercised and correct. The claim's mechanical repro is accurate — I reproduced its 5 warnings verbatim — but it fails every test my lens applies, and its core framing is inverted.

1) It changes nothing observable. `#![allow(...)]` is a lint level, not code. stdout is byte-identical across the C++ ground truth, the shipped /output/test6, and a rebuild with line 20 deleted, for 11 inputs including all the atoi edge cases (no arg, 0, 1, 6, 7, 100, -5, abc, 2147483648, 4294967296, 9223372036854775807). Exit statuses match. Both required build paths succeed with zero warnings as shipped: `cargo build --release --offline` and `rustc --edition 2021 -O test6.rs`. So it is not a compile failure, not a requirement failure (reqs 1-7 all hold), and not a behavioural defect. Per my lens that alone refutes it for this purpose.

2) The claim is self-refuting as a present defect, and I verified the admission independently. Its own repro text concedes "the attribute currently masks nothing in the lib". I confirmed that twice over: with the allow removed, `cargo build --release --offline --lib` emits zero warnings and still produces libsortedcontainers.rlib (so the lib target really is compiled, not skipped), and a standalone `rustc --edition 2021 --crate-type lib -O src/lib.rs` also emits zero warnings. There is no masked lib lint. The asserted harm is entirely about hypothetical dead private code someone might add later — a speculative style preference, not a defect in this artifact.

3) The "broader than the problem it solves" framing is backwards for the target that actually needs the allow. Because test6.rs pulls lib.rs in as a *module* (`#[path = "src/lib.rs"] mod sortedcontainers;`), the inner attribute scopes to that module subtree only — the bin's own code in test6.rs stays fully lint-checked. The remedy the claim implies (put the allow on the bin crate root instead) is strictly *broader*: I injected an unused import and a dead private fn into test6.rs in two variants. Current layout: 2 warnings correctly reported. Allow moved to the bin crate root: 0 warnings, both defects silenced. So the shipped placement gives tighter lint coverage exactly where lints do fire, while the proposed fix would blind the bin to its own dead code. lib.rs is also the only single site that covers both build modes (cargo crate root and rustc-included module) with one attribute, which is what the in-file comment on lines 17-19 documents.

Net: a nit whose stated downside is hypothetical, whose evidence concedes zero current effect, and whose obvious remedy is a regression in lint coverage. Not worth fixing.
